title: Cause and Effect Relationships
tagline: Year 3 — Deciding whether one event causes the other, both share a cause, or they are unrelated

introduction.overview: A cause-and-effect question gives two statements about events and asks how they are related. One may be the cause and the other the effect, both may be effects of a common cause, or they may be independent. The test is the time order and the direct link: a cause produces its effect, usually later; a common cause explains why two things happened together; and two statements with no link are independent.
introduction.placementRelevance: Cause-and-effect pairs are common in logical-reasoning sections and are quick to solve with a clear method.
introduction.realWorldContext: Tracing the root cause of a fault, a delay or a price change uses the same reasoning.

learningObjectives: Use time order and direct links
Recognise a common cause behind two effects

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A cause explains why the effect happened and usually comes before it in time.

coreDefinitions: Cause: an event that produces another event.
Common cause: one event that produces two separate effects.
Independent events: neither causes the other and there is no shared cause.
Immediate cause: the event just before the effect; principal cause: the root reason.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Try the sentence "I happened because II" and then "II happened because I". If neither sounds right but both sound like results of something else, look for a shared cause.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Say "because" both ways. If one direction fits and the other does not, you have cause and effect. If both are consequences of one hidden event, it is a common cause. If neither works, they are independent.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Because test
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: "A because B" fits one way only

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Independence
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Gold price and a film hit

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Reversal trap
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Do not confuse the result with the reason
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Holiday is the effect of the warning

mainNarrative: Heavy rain lashed the city for three days (I); many low-lying areas were waterlogged (II). "Waterlogged because of the rain" fits; "rain because of waterlogging" does not. I is the cause and II its effect.
A school holiday and a cyclone warning: the school declared a holiday because the warning was issued, so II is the cause and I its effect.

Many people in an area suffering from skin allergies and fish dying in the nearby river: neither causes the other, but one hidden cause such as factory discharge explains both. They are effects of a common cause.
A rise in the price of gold and a film becoming a box-office hit have no link in either direction and no shared cause. They are independent.
Beware of reversing the order. A bank cutting its lending rates after the central bank cuts its policy rate: the policy-rate cut is the cause (II), the lending-rate cut is the effect (I).

deepDiveAspects.title: Chains of causes
deepDiveAspects.content: When there is a chain A → B → C, the closer link is the immediate cause; the question usually asks only about the two given statements.

deepDiveAspects.title: Correlation is not causation
deepDiveAspects.content: Two events that occur together are not necessarily linked; the independent option exists for this reason.

solvedExamples.title: Direct cause
solvedExamples.question: I. Heavy rain lashed the city for three days. II. Many low-lying areas were waterlogged. How are they related?
solvedExamples.finalAnswer: I is the cause and II is its effect

solvedExamples.title: Common cause
solvedExamples.question: I. Many people in an area suffered from skin allergies. II. Fish died in large numbers in the nearby river. How are they related?

steps.title: Neither causes the other
steps.explanation: Allergies do not kill fish; dead fish do not cause allergies directly.

steps.title: Shared source
steps.explanation: Polluted water or discharge explains both.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: Both are effects of a common cause
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Environmental pollution is the likely common cause.

solvedExamples.title: Independent
solvedExamples.question: I. The price of gold rose sharply. II. A new film became a box-office hit. How are they related?

steps.title: Forward
steps.explanation: A rise in gold price does not produce a hit film.

steps.title: Backward
steps.explanation: A hit film does not raise gold prices, and no common cause is apparent.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: The two statements are independent of each other

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Say "because" both ways; one-way fit means cause and effect, both being results of a hidden event means common cause, no fit means independent.

placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Look for words such as announced, decided, imposed (usually causes).
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Policy decisions usually come before their consequences.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I find a common cause?
Can I call two events independent?
